question: Natura 2000 protects invaluable natural habitats across the EU. It is a fundamental part of the EU’s ability to protect biodiversity and a rich natural environment because environmental problems take no heed of national borders. The EU’s system is really put to the test, however, in times when there is a lot of pressure for development.

In the name of competitiveness, a number of parties, including Parliament’s largest political group, the EPP, are calling for Natura 2000 to be overhauled. At the same time, more exploration permits are being granted for development in protected areas.

There are several examples of this in Jämtland (Sweden), including Jänsmässholmen, Lake Näkten and Hårkan – three examples of areas with sensitive habitats that are important for reindeer herding, outdoor recreation and red‑list species. Increasing pressure for development is threatening to undermine the conservation objectives that the Member States have to meet in Natura 2000 sites.

Given that a number of stakeholders are wrongly pitting nature conservation against competitiveness – something that the responsible Commissioner has repeatedly emphasised is not a real contradiction – I should like to ask: 1.
How is the Commission, alongside the Member States, intending to ensure that Europe’s biodiversity is protected?
Can the Commission confirm that there are no plans to place restrictions on Natura 2000 or on the Habitats Directive?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.7.2026) Biodiversity protection in the EU is firmly grounded in the implementation and enforcement of the EU Birds1 and Habitats Directives2 and the Natura 2000 network, among other legal instruments.

According to Article 6(3) of the Habitats Directive, any plan or project likely to have a significant negative effect on a Natura 2000 site, either individually or in combination with other plans or projects, must be subject to an appropriate assessment of its implications for the site in view of the site’s conservation objectives and can only be approved if it will not adversely affect the integrity of the site concerned.

Exceptions to this obligation may be accepted under the conditions established in Article 6(4). Building on this framework, the Nature Restoration Regulation3 delivers on the commitment taken under the EU Biodiversity Strategy for 20304 and the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework5 by setting legally binding restoration targets across ecosystems.

Together with Member States, the Commission will continue to support effective implementation, financing, monitoring and enforcement measures to halt biodiversity loss, restore degraded ecosystems and strengthen the resilience of Europe’s natural capital for future generations.

The Commission is currently carrying out a stress test of the Birds and Habitats Directives6 as part of its wider initiative on simplification. The stress test aims to evaluate whether the Directives remain fit to achieve their objectives in a cost-efficient way, while maintaining their ambition and high standards of nature conservation.
The results – planned for end 2026 – will form the basis for the Commission to decide on the appropriate follow up.
1 Directive 2009/147/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 November 2009 on the

conservation of wild birds, OJ L 20, 26.1.2010, p. 7–25. 2 Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora, OJ L 206, 22.7.1992, p. 7–50. 3 Regulation (EU) 2024/1991 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 June 2024 on nature restoration and amending Regulation (EU) 2022/869, OJ L, 2024/1991, 29.7.2024. 4 https://environment.ec.europa.
